title: What Does the Church Owe People With Disabilities?
subtitle: A culture that measures human worth by usefulness, independence, and the flawless body has no honest place for the disabled, and too often the church has quietly agreed. Scripture says something the world cannot say. That the image of God is borne fully by every body, that strength is made perfect in weakness, that the parts we think weaker are indispensable, and that a community which has no room for the different body is not yet the body of Christ.

connections.label: Health, Illness, and Pain: the long endurance of a body that does not work as hoped
Identity and Worth: where dignity comes from when the body cannot earn it
The Church as Family: belonging that does not depend on ability
Suffering and the Silence of God: the hard questions a different body raises
Take stock of how your community includes the whole body with the life audit

parts.title: The Real Struggle
parts.body:
The ramp is around the back, past the dumpsters, and the family in the wheelchair takes it every Sunday because the front steps were built for bodies that climb. The mother of the boy who cannot sit still through a service has stopped coming, not because she stopped believing but because she ran out of strength for the looks. The man whose stroke took his speech sits in the back and no one asks him anything anymore, because asking takes patience and the line for coffee is long. These are not stories from a hard place. These are stories from the church down the street, and from mine.

We live in a culture that has decided, without ever saying it aloud, that the worth of a human being is measured by what the body can do. Useful, independent, productive, attractive, capable, the words our age uses for a good life are all words the different body cannot fully claim. And so the person whose body does not work the way bodies are supposed to work lives under a quiet, constant verdict, delivered not in cruelty but in a thousand small absences. The party they were not invited to. The job they did not get. The conversation that flowed around them as though they were furniture. The world built for other bodies, by people who never thought of theirs.

I am not writing this from outside the failure. I am a pastor, and I have built services that the deaf could not follow and planned events the wheelchair could not reach. I have been the one who found it easier to talk to the caregiver than to the person, who let the awkwardness of a different body push me toward the easy exit of a quick hello. I have preached that every person bears the image of God and then arranged a church life that quietly assumed everyone could walk in, sit still, and follow along. The failure is not theirs. It is ours, and it is mine.

There is a particular loneliness that the different body knows, and it is not mainly the loneliness of the limitation itself. It is the loneliness of being a problem. Of feeling that your presence is an accommodation rather than a gift, that the room adjusted to fit you and resented the adjusting, that you are tolerated where you long to be wanted. The world tells the disabled person, in ways subtle and gross, that they are a burden, a cost, a complication, a life of diminished value, and the most haunting thing is how often the church has failed to say anything different, has met the different body with pity instead of welcome, with a project of fixing instead of a place at the table.

And underneath all of it runs the hardest question of all, the one whispered in the dark by the person whose body will not heal and by the parent whose child will not be made well. Where is God in this body. Does he see it, value it, want it. Is a life like this a mistake he is sorry for, or a life he made and called his own. The culture has an answer, and the answer is no. The question is whether the church has a better one, and whether it has the courage to live it.

parts.title: Why It Matters
parts.body:
Because the way a society treats its weakest members is the truest measure of what it actually believes about human worth, and our society is failing the test in ways that should frighten us. When the value of a life is pegged to its usefulness, the lives that are least useful become, by the cold logic of the system, the most expendable, and we are watching that logic work itself out in real time. Where I write, more than nine in ten children diagnosed before birth with Down syndrome are never allowed to be born. That is not a statistic about medicine. It is a verdict about worth, and it is the verdict the whole culture is quietly rendering on the different body. The stakes here are not sensitivity. The stakes are whether some human beings count as human at all.

It matters because the church has too often been complicit in the very devaluing it should resist. We have built our buildings, our services, our programs, and our whole sense of normal around the able body, and then wondered why the disabled feel unwelcome. We have treated disability as a problem to be solved by healing rather than a person to be loved in the meantime, leaving the unhealed feeling like a failure of faith. We have offered pity where we owed honor, and accommodation where we owed belonging, and we have done it while preaching a gospel that says the last shall be first and the weak shame the strong. The gap between what we preach and how we build our churches is a scandal, and the people in the wheelchairs and the back rows can see it more clearly than we can.

It matters because what you believe about the different body is what you believe about your own. Disability is not a category that divides the healthy from the afflicted. It is a country every one of us is traveling toward, slowly or suddenly, by age or accident, and the only question is when we arrive. The culture that despises the weak body is teaching every person in it to despise the body they will one day have, to dread their own aging and frailty as a descent into worthlessness. A community that honors the different body is teaching every member that they will still be loved when their own body fails, and that is a promise every human being needs and only the gospel can keep.

It matters because the church does not merely tolerate the different body. The church needs it. Paul says the parts of the body we think are weaker are indispensable, that God has arranged things so the members care for one another, and that the suffering of one is the suffering of all. This is not sentiment. It is structure. A church without its disabled members is not a complete church being generous to the incomplete. It is an incomplete church missing parts it cannot do without, deprived of gifts and graces and a witness that only the different body carries. To exclude is not only to wound the excluded. It is to maim ourselves.

And it matters because the watching world is looking for one place that does not run on the cruel arithmetic of usefulness, one community where a person is loved for being and not for doing, where the weak are not hidden but honored, where a life that the culture has written off is received as a gift. If the church cannot be that place, there is no place, and the gospel's claim that every person is made in the image of God and loved by him is just words. The different body is where that claim gets tested. The world is watching to see whether we mean it.

parts.title: The Biblical Vision
parts.body:
The Bible opens with a sentence that the culture cannot say and the church must never stop saying. God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him. The text draws no line. It does not say the strong body bears the image and the weak body bears a fraction of it. The image of God is borne fully, equally, irreducibly by every human being, by the body that runs and the body that cannot rise, by the mind that calculates and the mind that will never read, and this single sentence demolishes the entire foundation on which our culture builds its hierarchy of worth. Every person is a king or queen wearing the image of the Maker, and no diagnosis, no limitation, no different way of being a body can subtract a single degree of that glory.

Then watch how God reveals himself, and notice that he keeps choosing the weak. He picks Moses, who pleads that he is slow of speech and slow of tongue, and God answers with a question that should silence every assumption we make about ability. Who has made man's mouth. Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind. Is it not I, the Lord. God does not promise to fix Moses. He claims Moses as he is, stammer and all, and sends him. The God of the Bible is not embarrassed by the different body. He made it, he owns it, and he has a track record of doing his greatest work through exactly the people the world counts out.

Look at how the law of God treats the disabled, in an ancient world that routinely abandoned them. You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God. In a culture that mocked and discarded the weak, Israel was commanded to protect them and to ground that protection in the fear of God himself. The vulnerable body was not a defect to be hidden but a neighbor to be honored, and the way you treated it was reckoned as the way you treated God.

Then comes Jesus, and the way he meets the different body breaks every category. He touches the leper that no one would touch. He stops the entire procession for the blind beggar that the crowd was shushing. He has a particular tenderness for exactly the bodies the world averted its eyes from, and when his disciples look at a man born blind and ask whose sin caused it, assuming the disability must be a punishment, Jesus refuses the whole premise. It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. He will not let them read the different body as a verdict of guilt. He reads it instead as a place where the glory of God will be seen. And when he describes the great feast of the kingdom, he says go out and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame, not as charity cases admitted to the edges but as the honored guests the host actually wanted at his table.

And here is the deepest thing the Bible says, the thing that turns the whole world's logic upside down. The gospel does not run on strength. It runs on weakness. Paul begged God three times to remove his thorn, his weakness, his affliction, and God refused, and gave him instead a word that has carried the disabled and the suffering for two thousand years. My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. So Paul learns to boast in his weaknesses, because when he is weak, then he is strong. This is not a consolation prize for those who cannot have strength. This is the actual architecture of the kingdom, in which God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, in which the treasure is carried in jars of clay so the power is seen to be from God and not from us. The crucified Christ, broken and helpless on a cross, is the power of God for salvation. The different body is not at the margins of this gospel. It is near its center, a living parable of the truth that God's strength is shown in weakness, and that the body the world calls less is the body through which God delights to display himself.

And Paul writes the church a vision of itself that leaves no one out. The body of Christ has many members, and the eye cannot say to the hand I have no need of you. On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and the parts we think less honorable we clothe with greater honor. God has so composed the body that there may be no division, that the members may have the same care for one another, that if one suffers all suffer together. This is the charter of a church that has room for the different body, and it is not a charter of pity. It is a charter of need. The church is not whole until the weak are not merely admitted but honored, not tolerated but treasured, not at the back but at the center, because the body of Christ is a body in which every part is necessary and the parts the world would discard are the ones God calls indispensable. And the last word is the best word, the promise that one day there will be a new creation in which the lame leap and the blind see and the mute sing, not because the different body was a mistake God finally corrected, but because every body, made for glory, will at last be raised to the wholeness it was always meant for, by the One who became weak to make the weak strong forever.

parts.title: The Historical and Traditional Wisdom
parts.body:
The ancient world into which the church was born was merciless to the different body. The Greeks and Romans practiced the exposure of disabled infants, leaving the weak newborn on a hillside to die, and the great philosophers approved. Plato and Aristotle both endorsed the abandonment of the deformed and the sickly as a matter of civic health, and the wider culture saw disability as a sign of the gods' displeasure, a shame to be hidden or a defect to be discarded. This was the normal of the ancient world, the cold arithmetic of usefulness applied without apology to the bodies that could not measure up.

Into that world came a community that did something unprecedented. The early Christians took in the abandoned infants the Romans left to die, gathered the sick the city cast out, and treated the disabled as bearers of the image of God rather than as refuse. When plagues swept the cities and the healthy fled, the Christians stayed and nursed the dying, and the watching pagan world could not account for it. The emperor Julian, who hated the faith and tried to revive paganism in the fourth century, complained bitterly that the Christians cared not only for their own poor and sick but for everyone's, and that this care was winning the world. The honoring of the weak body was, from the beginning, one of the most visible and disruptive marks of the church.

The Christian centuries built the institutions that this conviction required. The hospital, in any form we would recognize, is a Christian invention, born of the belief that the sick and the disabled were Christ himself to be served, on the strength of his own words that whatever you did for the least of these you did for me. Basil of Caesarea built a whole complex for the sick and the poor in the fourth century. The monasteries became refuges for the infirm, places where the body that could not keep up was kept and fed and honored within a community. The medieval church, for all its failures, carried a conviction the ancient world never had, that the weak body was not to be exposed on a hillside but received as a guest of Christ.

Later the church learned to listen more closely, and to repent of the ways it had failed even while it served. There were centuries when disability was wrongly read as demonic, when the church confused the different body with a spiritual problem and added cruelty to the wound. The tradition had to be corrected by Scripture again and again, called back from pity to honor, from fixing to belonging. In the modern era voices like Jean Vanier, who founded the L'Arche communities in 1964 where people with and without intellectual disabilities live together as equals, recovered the radical biblical insight that the church does not merely serve the disabled but needs them, that the so-called weak members carry gifts of presence, of joy, of unguarded love that the capable and the busy have lost. The theologian Henri Nouwen left a celebrated academic career to live in such a community, and wrote that the disabled men and women there taught him more about the gospel than the universities ever had, because they could not earn love and so revealed it for the gift it always was.

And the modern world stands at a fork the ancient world would recognize. The exposure of the disabled infant on the hillside has returned, in cleaner clothing, as a culture that screens out the different body before birth and calls the elimination compassion. The same logic that left the weak newborn to die has come back wearing the language of choice and health and quality of life, and it is winning, quietly, by the millions. The church that once shocked the empire by gathering the abandoned is called again to be a sign of contradiction, to insist against the whole drift of the age that every body bears the image of God, that the weak are indispensable, and that a community which has no room for the different body has forgotten the One who was born in a stable and died on a cross precisely to dignify the bodies the world throws away. The vision will have to be lived again, deliberately, against the grain, the way it was lived the first time, one welcomed and honored person at a time.

parts.title: The Honest Engagement with Knowledge
parts.body: Christians have much to learn from the disability rights movement, from the field of disability studies, and from the hard-won wisdom of disabled people themselves about how the world is built and who it leaves out. All truth is God's truth, and the secular advocates have seen things the church was slow to see, the way our environments exclude, the dignity the able-bodied take for granted, the difference between pity and respect. But every account of the different body carries a hidden picture of where human worth comes from, and that is where the testing happens. So we read these honest observers with gratitude, and then we test what they say against Scripture, keeping what is true and correcting what is aimed wrong.

secular.author: Michael Oliver and the disability rights movement
secular.whatItGetsRight: Oliver and the disability rights movement made a distinction the church should have made first, between impairment, the actual condition of a body, and disability, the way a society built for other bodies turns that condition into exclusion. The stairs, not the legs, are what keep the wheelchair out of the building. This insight relocates the problem from the disabled person, who is told to adapt or be fixed, to the community that built a world assuming everyone was the same, and it has driven enormous and genuinely good change, ramps and rights and the slow dismantling of barriers nobody used to notice.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The social model rightly indicts the exclusion and stops short of naming where the dignity it defends actually comes from. It can tell society to remove the barriers and cannot tell society why the person behind the barrier is worth removing them for, leaving the worth of the disabled to rest on the shifting ground of social agreement. Scripture grounds the dignity it cannot, in the image of God borne fully by every body, so that the wheelchair user is not owed access because society has decided to be inclusive but because he is a bearer of the divine image whose honor was never society's to grant or withhold. The model fixes the building. Scripture tells you who lives in it.

secular.source: Disability theology and the vulnerable body
secular.author: Nancy Eiesland and theological disability studies
secular.whatItGetsRight: Eiesland, in 1994, pressed the church to see disability not as a problem at the edge of theology but as a lens at its center, and recovered the startling truth that the risen Christ still bears his wounds. The resurrected body of Jesus is a body that was broken and remains marked, scars in the hands and side, which means that disability is not simply erased in the kingdom but in some sense taken up into glory. Her work forced the church to confront how thoroughly it had built its theology and its buildings around the able body, and to hear the disabled as theologians of their own experience rather than objects of its charity.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Eiesland sees the wounded Christ truly and at points presses the image past what Scripture will bear, when the emphasis on disability as permanent identity strains against the promise that the lame shall leap and the mute shall sing. Scripture holds both together more carefully than either the cult of cure or the refusal of all healing. The wounds of the risen Christ are real and glorified, a sign that suffering is not wasted, and the new creation is still a place of wholeness where every tear is wiped away. The believer is neither told his body is a mistake to be erased nor that his impairment is his eternal essence, but that he, the whole person, is loved now and will be raised whole, his scars redeemed rather than denied.

secular.author: Andrew Solomon
secular.whatItGetsRight: Solomon, in 2012, spent a decade interviewing families raising children profoundly different from themselves, including children with severe disabilities, and documented with extraordinary honesty both the genuine suffering and the genuine love, the way families who expected only tragedy found unexpected meaning, and the fierce dignity parents came to see in children the world had written off. He refuses the easy narratives in both directions, neither pretending the hardship away nor reducing the child to it, and he honors the love that learns to receive a child as a gift rather than a disappointment.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Solomon documents the love that families discover and locates its source finally in human meaning-making, the family's own heroic decision to find value where the world saw none. Scripture says the value was there before anyone decided to see it, woven in at creation, so that the parents are not bravely assigning worth to a child who lacks it but slowly waking up to a worth that was always there. This matters under pressure, because a dignity the family must generate can fail when the family is exhausted, while a dignity given by God holds even when human love runs dry. Solomon honors the love. Scripture secures the ground beneath it.

secular.source: Being Disabled and the ethics of independence
secular.author: Eva Feder Kittay and the ethics of care
secular.whatItGetsRight: Kittay, a philosopher and the mother of a profoundly disabled daughter, exposed the lie at the heart of how modern culture measures worth, the idol of independence. She argues that the picture of the valuable human being as the autonomous, self-sufficient individual is a fiction that excludes the most dependent among us and, in truth, describes none of us, since every human being begins and ends in total dependence and lives the whole middle in webs of care. Her recovery of dependence as a normal and dignified human condition cuts directly against the cult of self-sufficiency that the disabled are measured against and found wanting.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Kittay dismantles the idol of independence and reaches, without quite naming it, a truth Scripture states outright. Dependence is not the disabled person's tragedy but the human condition, for every creature is dependent first and always upon God, who gives breath and being moment by moment to the strong and the weak alike. The cult of self-sufficiency the disabled are crushed under is a lie told to everyone, the able-bodied most of all, who imagine an autonomy they do not possess. Scripture frees the disabled from the false standard not merely by widening the definition of the human but by confessing that all of us are dependent creatures held by a Father, so that the most dependent person is not furthest from the human ideal but closest to its truth.

secular.author: Joseph Shapiro
secular.whatItGetsRight: Shapiro, in 1993, gave voice to a generation of disabled people insisting that they did not want pity, did not see themselves as tragic, and refused the role of the suffering inspiration the able-bodied wanted to cast them in. He documented the disability rights movement's demand to be treated as full citizens and full persons rather than as objects of charity or sentiment, and his central insight, that pity is a form of condescension that denies equality, named something the church has been guilty of for centuries when it offered the disabled sympathy instead of fellowship.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Shapiro rightly refuses pity and replaces it with the demand for equal rights, which is good and incomplete, because rights can secure a place in society without securing a place at a table, and a person can be granted equality and still be profoundly alone. Scripture refuses pity too and offers something deeper than rights, which is belonging, the welcome of the poor and the crippled and the lame as honored guests at the feast, members of a body who are not merely equal but indispensable and loved. The disabled person in the church is owed not the cool respect of equal citizenship but the warm honor of a brother or sister whom the body cannot do without. Rights make you a citizen. The gospel makes you family.

parts.title: Where Faithful People Differ
parts.body: Faithful Christians who agree that the different body bears the full image of God still differ on how to hold healing and acceptance together, and the difference is not careless. It runs to whether the believing response to disability should lean toward earnest prayer for healing and the hope of restoration, or toward the peaceful acceptance of the body as God has given it. Hear each at its strongest, because both are reading the same Scripture, which both prays for healing and promises grace sufficient in weakness, and each is guarding against a real danger that wounds the disabled when the other view is held carelessly.

views.view: The hope of healing, praying earnestly for restoration
views.body: This view holds that the Christian should pray boldly and persistently for the healing of the different body, because Scripture is full of a God who heals, because Jesus made the lame walk and the blind see as a sign of the kingdom breaking in, and because the new creation itself is a promise that brokenness is not the final word over any body. It points to the many times Jesus healed, to his command to pray for the sick, to the church's long ministry of laying on hands and asking God to restore, and it insists that to stop praying for healing is to stop believing that God still does what he did in the Gospels. The conviction underneath is that disability, whatever good God works through it, is finally a part of the brokenness that Christ came to undo, and that hoping and praying for its undoing is faith rather than discontent. Advocates warn against a resignation that gives up too soon, that baptizes every limitation as God's settled will and quietly stops asking him for more, and they hold up instead the bold faith that brings every need to a Father who can do more than we ask. The danger they are most careful to guard against, when they hold this view rightly, is the cruelty of a healing theology that blames the unhealed, that tells the person still in the wheelchair their faith was too small, and so they pray for healing while insisting, always, that the failure of healing to come is never the sufferer's fault and never a measure of their standing with God, who loves the unhealed body as fully as the restored one.

views.view: The grace of acceptance, receiving the body as God has given it
views.body: This view holds that the deepest Christian response to the different body is to receive it in peace as a body God knew and loved and made his own, and to find, as Paul did, that grace is sufficient and that God's power is made perfect in the very weakness that is not taken away. It points to Paul's thorn, prayed over three times and left in place by a God who said his grace was enough, to the man born blind whose condition was not a punishment but a stage for the works of God, and to the whole gospel logic in which the weak are not waiting to become strong but are the place where God's strength is shown. The conviction underneath is that the constant pressure to be healed can itself become a burden, a message to the disabled that they are unacceptable as they are, a life on hold until a restoration that may never come, and that the gospel offers instead a present and unconditional belonging that does not depend on the body changing. Advocates warn against a healing culture that treats the different body as a problem to be solved rather than a person to be loved, that makes the unhealed feel like failures, and they hold up instead the dignity of a life received whole, now, as it is. The danger they are most careful to guard against, when they hold this view rightly, is a fatalism that stops caring, that uses acceptance as an excuse to abandon the disabled to their limitations and withhold the help and the prayer they may genuinely want, and so they receive the body in peace while still longing, with the whole groaning creation, for the day when every body is raised whole.

parts.title: The Formation
parts.body:
The different body forms the whole community around it, not only the person who bears it, and this is the truth the church has been slowest to learn. We imagine the disabled person as the one being formed, by patience, by dependence, by the long endurance of a body that does not cooperate, and that is true and not the half of it. The deeper work is what the different body forms in everyone near it, in a church, in a family, in a friend, if that community will receive the gift instead of managing the problem. The presence of the weak member is not a drain on the body of Christ. It is one of the chief means by which the body of Christ is made into the body of Christ.

It forms in the strong a humility they could learn no other way. The able-bodied live under the great illusion of self-sufficiency, the lie that they are independent, capable, in control, and the different body quietly tells the truth that every body will eventually tell, that we are all dependent creatures held moment by moment by a strength not our own. To love a person who cannot pretend to self-sufficiency is to have your own pretense exposed, gently, and to be set free from the exhausting performance of not needing anyone. The disabled member is, among other things, a prophet to the able, preaching by their very existence the truth that the strong spend their lives denying, that to be human is to be dependent, and that there is no shame in it, only the dignity of a creature held by its Maker.

It forms a love that cannot be earned and so reveals what love actually is. The relationships of the able-bodied world run, mostly, on exchange, on the quiet calculation of what each person brings, and we rarely notice how much our love is a transaction until we are asked to love someone who cannot repay it, who will never make us look good, who can offer us nothing the market values. The person with a profound disability cannot earn love, and so they expose it, stripping away the exchange and leaving only the gift, teaching the community that learns to love them what grace has meant all along, a love that is given to those who cannot deserve it, by a God whose love for us was never a transaction either. Henri Nouwen said the disabled taught him the gospel the universities could not, and this is why. They could not earn his love, and so they showed him what love is.

And it forms a true picture of the kingdom, where the last are first and the weak are indispensable and the parts the world discards are the ones God honors. A church that has learned to treasure its different bodies is a church being formed into the shape of its crucified Lord, who was himself the weak one, the broken body, the despised and rejected man through whom God saved the world. The different body is not a deviation from the gospel that the church must work around. It is a living parable of the gospel's deepest truth, that God's power is made perfect in weakness, that he chose what is weak to shame the strong, that the treasure is carried in jars of clay. The community that welcomes and honors the weak body is being slowly conformed to the image of the One who became weak to save it, and is learning, in the only way it can be learned, that strength was never the point, and that the body of Christ is whole only when its weakest members are not at the back but at the center, where the Lord himself has always placed them. The formation, in the end, is the making of a community that looks like its Savior, broken and beloved, weak and full of grace, with room at the table for every body, because the One who set the table has room for them all.

parts.title: The Practice
parts.body: None of what follows is a program for fixing the different body or a checklist for feeling better about disability. It is about becoming, person by person and church by church, the community Scripture describes, where every body is honored and no one is a problem to be managed. A few things must be said plainly first. If you are caring for a disabled child or spouse or parent and you are drowning, the exhaustion is real and the grief is allowed, and seeking help, respite, counseling, and the support of others is faith and not failure. If you carry a different body yourself and the loneliness or the despair has become a darkness you cannot lift, please reach for a doctor and a counselor as well as a friend, because some weights are not meant to be carried alone. And if you are a church, understand that good intentions have left the disabled outside your doors for generations, and only deliberate, costly change will bring them in. Start where you are, with one thing, and let the rest come as you learn.

steps: Talk to the person, not around them. This week, find the one in the wheelchair or the back row or the family everyone steps past, and speak to them directly, ask them a real question, and wait for the answer however long it takes. Treat them as a person with a name, not a condition with a caregiver.

Notice one barrier you have never noticed. Walk your church or your home as though you used a wheelchair, could not hear, or could not follow a fast-moving room, and name one thing built for other bodies that quietly keeps someone out. Seeing the barrier is the first repentance.

Examine your own heart for pity dressed as kindness. Ask honestly whether you offer the disabled sympathy from a safe distance instead of fellowship up close, and whether your discomfort with a different body has been pushing you toward the easy exit. Name it before God.

Read John 9 slowly, and let Jesus refuse the question your culture keeps asking. It was not that this man sinned, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. Let it dismantle, in you, the assumption that the different body is a verdict rather than a person God made and loves.

Move one relationship from accommodation to friendship. Pick one disabled person in your life or your church and pursue them as a friend rather than a project, not to help them but to know them, to receive what they have to give rather than only to give what you think they need.

Learn the story behind one different body, with permission and without intrusion. Ask a disabled person or a caregiving family what they actually need, what they wish the church understood, what would make them feel wanted rather than tolerated, and then listen without rushing to fix.

Examine where your sense of your own worth secretly rests on your ability, and let the different body teach you. Sit with the question of whether you would still know yourself loved if your body failed tomorrow, and let the answer drive you back to the image of God as the ground of worth that no body can lose.

If you are a caregiver, accept one piece of help this month that you have been refusing. The strength to care for a different body is not infinite, and receiving help is not weakness but wisdom, the very dependence you are learning to honor in the one you care for.

Work to change one real barrier in your church, and accept that it will cost something. A ramp at the front instead of behind the dumpsters. A quiet room for the family with the child who cannot sit still. A way for the deaf to follow the sermon. Belonging is built in concrete and not only in feeling.

Build a place at the center, not the edge, for the different bodies in your community. Move them from being served to serving, from being ministered to toward ministering, because the gifts of the weak members are real and the church is poorer without them. Ask what they have to give, and then let them give it.

Sit honestly with the hard questions this season raises, neither pretending them away nor letting them have the last word. Where is God in this body. Why this child, this stroke, this diagnosis. Bring the lament to God who can bear it, and let Paul's thorn and Christ's wounds keep company with your unanswered questions.

If you carry a different body, practice receiving your own dignity as a gift this season, not earning it and not waiting on a healing to claim it. You bear the image of God now, fully, and you are loved now, fully, and the strength of God is being made perfect in your weakness now, not someday.

Make your church, your family, or your circle a place where the different body is not merely admitted but treasured, and measure your progress not by your intentions but by whether the disabled actually come, stay, belong, and lead. A community is known by who is at its center, and the gospel puts the weak there.

Become, over years, the kind of person whose love does not run on exchange, who can love the one who cannot repay, who has learned from the different body what grace has meant all along. Let the people the world counts least teach you the gospel the universities cannot.

Stand against the cruel arithmetic of the age, the logic that screens out and writes off the different body before it is even born, and bear public witness, with your votes and your money and your welcome, that every body bears the image of God and counts as fully human. The church that once shocked the empire by gathering the abandoned is called to it again.

Keep returning to the One the different body is pointing at, the crucified Christ who was himself the weak one, the broken body, the despised and rejected man through whom God saved the world. Let the weakness around you and within you preach the gospel's deepest truth, that God's strength is made perfect in weakness, until the day the lame leap and the blind see and every body is raised whole by the One who became weak to make the weak strong forever.
